title: Assets and liabilities: getting it right, without going to extremes.
subtitle: An asset puts money in your pocket; a liability takes money out of it.
openingQuestion: Is the house you live in an asset or a liability?
openingOptions: An asset, because it has value
Neither an asset nor a liability
It depends on your point of view
A liability, because it takes money out (tax, upkeep, the loan)
explanation: The same house can be an asset or a liability, depending on whether it puts money into your pocket or takes it out. The house you live in generates negative cash flow every month: loan interest, tax, management fees, repairs. A rented-out house generates positive cash flow. This doesn't mean buying a home to live in is wrong - it meets a real need - it just means don't mistake it for an investment when you're counting how many things are actually supporting you.

diagram.label: Does it put money in or take money out each month?
In: an asset. Out: a liability
The same object can switch groups when its use changes

realWorldExample.description: A personal car is a textbook liability: insurance, petrol, upkeep, depreciation every year. A taxi is an asset: it generates income.

quiz.question: By the cash-flow definition, what is an asset?
options: Anything that has a resale value on the market
Something that generates positive cash flow or grows in value for you
Something that has your name on its legal papers
The cash, gold, stocks and other securities currently sitting in your possession
quiz.explanation: From a cash-flow perspective: an asset is something that puts money into your pocket. Dividend-paying stocks, a rented-out flat, or a skill that raises your income all count as assets in this sense.

quiz.question: What goes wrong when the view that 'the home you live in is a liability' is taken to an extreme?
options: It ignores non-financial value (a settled home, stability) and real estate's long-term potential to appreciate
That view only holds in developing countries and doesn't apply to Vietnam's market
It's wrong because it only affects high earners, so ordinary people needn't care
Nothing is wrong with it; the cash-flow view applies absolutely, with no exceptions at all
quiz.explanation: Personal finance isn't only about optimising cash flow. Having a settled home, psychological stability, and long-term price appreciation all carry real value. Any extreme leads to a skewed decision.

quiz.question: Scenario: You have 200 million VND. Option A: buy a personal motorbike (insurance, petrol, upkeep cost roughly 5 million a year). Option B: buy a motorbike to drive for Grab (income roughly 15 million a year after costs). By the cash-flow definition, which option is an asset?
options: A is an asset, because a personal bike still has resale value
B is an asset, because it generates 15 million a year of positive cash flow
Both are assets, because both currently have some resale value on the open market
Neither is an asset, because a motorbike always depreciates
quiz.explanation: By the cash-flow definition: an asset is something that puts money into your pocket. The Grab bike generates 15 million a year of positive cash flow, so it's an asset. The personal bike takes out 5 million a year, so it's a liability. The same kind of bike, a different use, a different outcome.

quiz.question: The same car - under what condition does it count as an asset by the cash-flow definition?
options: When it's used for a service and earnings exceed running costs
When it's bought outright with no loan, so no interest is incurred
When its price on the used market is still high
When it belongs to a model that holds its value well after years
quiz.explanation: The classification lies in how it's used, not in the object itself. The very same car, used for personal travel, costs petrol, insurance and upkeep every month; run as a paid service that turns a profit, it pumps money into your pocket instead.

quiz.question: Scenario: You buy a 2 billion VND flat to rent out. Rent collected comes to 8 million a month, while management fees plus loan interest run to 11 million a month. By the cash-flow definition, what is this?
options: An asset, because real estate always appreciates over the long run
A liability, because it pulls 3 million out of your pocket every month
An asset, because it generates a steady stream of rental income
A liability, but only once it's actually been sold at a realized capital loss
quiz.explanation: Generating revenue doesn't automatically make something an asset: taking in 8 while paying out 11 means your pocket is 3 million lighter every month. Expected appreciation might make up for it later, but that's a bet on price, not on cash flow - and while you wait, you still have to cover 3 million every month.

keyTakeaways: An asset generates positive cash flow; a liability generates negative cash flow
The same object can be an asset or a liability depending on how it's used
Avoid extremes: life isn't only a cash-flow optimisation problem

practicePrompt.question: How could a personal motorbike become an asset?
options: By being kept parked in the garage, unused
It can never become an asset
By being used to commute to work and earn extra income
By being used only for personal needs, generating ongoing costs
practicePrompt.explanation: Once something generates value or cash flow, it becomes an asset in the financial sense. How it's used decides whether it delivers a benefit.

summary.keyIdea: Something can be an asset or a liability depending on how it affects your cash flow.
summary.formula: Asset = something that puts money into your pocket or grows in value long-term.
summary.commonMistake: Looking at book value while ignoring actual cash flow.
summary.action: Look back at three things you own and ask: which ones are putting money in, which ones are taking it out?

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Don't just ask 'is this worth the money?'; ask 'does this make me richer or poorer each month?'.

sections.text: The house you live in - asset or liability? The answer isn't fixed; it depends on how you use it.
Defined by cash flow, not by feeling

The most precise definition (from Robert Kiyosaki, widely used in personal finance): an asset is something that puts money into your pocket (generates positive cash flow), a liability is something that takes money out of your pocket (generates negative cash flow). This is a definition based on actual cash flow, not market value or the feeling of 'owning something valuable'.
The same object, two different roles

The home you live in generates negative cash flow every month: loan interest, property tax, upkeep fees - all money flowing out, with no money flowing in to offset it (unless the price rises and you sell). By the cash-flow definition, this is a liability, even though its market value may rise over time. A rented-out flat, by contrast, generates monthly rent exceeding its running costs - a genuine asset.

items: The home you live in: negative cash flow (loan interest, tax, upkeep) → a liability by the cash-flow definition
A profitable rental property: positive cash flow → an asset
A personal car: depreciates and costs upkeep → a liability
A stock that pays steady dividends: positive cash flow → an asset

sections.label: Don't take it to extremes
sections.text: This definition is a thinking tool, not a rule to live by. A home to live in still carries huge non-financial value: stability, a settled life, family happiness. Life isn't only a cash-flow optimisation problem - don't sell the home you live in just because it is 'technically a liability'.

lines: Understanding the asset-liability framework correctly helps you weigh big decisions more clearly, but don't let it fully replace the other non-financial values that matter in life.
